sections.html:
Three separate groups share the work in this county. Commissioners and city boards choose the rates. The Property Assessor sets what a parcel is worth. The Trustee handles bills and payments. You will find the Trustee in Suite 203 at 1320 West Main Street, Franklin (zip 37064), reachable at 615-790-5709, with the counter open weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30. If your question is about value or a mailing address, dial the Assessor instead at 615-790-5708.

The Trustee's bill covers Williamson County, the Franklin Special School District, Brentwood, Franklin, Nolensville and Thompson's Station. Spring Hill and Fairview owners get their city charge elsewhere, so a quick call to city hall tells you who sends it.

Leniency is not on offer here. T.C.A. 67-5-2803 strips the Trustee of any power to waive, prorate or release tax or interest, so a late bill simply stays late.

This is a high-value Middle Tennessee market. The population reached 272,061 in July 2025, a 9.8% rise over the April 2020 base. There are 103,674 housing units, and owners live in 78.8% of the occupied ones. A typical owned home is valued at $751,900, and builders pulled 1,621 permits in 2025. Brentwood and Franklin anchor the north end, while the south keeps more of its farm feel. Williamson County Schools serves most of the county, and part of Franklin sends kindergarten through eighth graders to the Franklin Special School District.

Tennessee fixes the share of appraised value that gets taxed: 25 percent on a house, 40 percent on commercial and industrial buildings, 30 percent on business personal property. Your rate multiplies each $100 of that taxed share, so a bigger appraisal means a bigger bill. Your appraisal is the number worth checking, because everything else follows from it.

The 2026 rates appear as a chart on the county's Property Tax Rates page. Add the county rate to whichever city or school district covers your address to see the full picture. New construction is valued through September 1, and then the rolls move to the Trustee.

The roll goes public in May. If your value changed, a notice arrives by mail. Reading it right away leaves time to act before hearings begin in June.

The Trustee mails statements in early October. Paying costs nothing extra from the first Monday of that month through February's last day, and you may split the payment into installments. On March 1 the Trustee tacks on 1.5 percent, then repeats that at the start of each later month. A bill is good for one calendar year only.

Escrow customers still get a statement, which the Trustee calls a copy for your records. Phone ahead to learn which payment methods the 2026 bill accepts, and take the bill or your parcel details if you pay in person.

Two rules matter once you plan to sell. The mailing follows whoever owned the parcel on January 1, so a seller who has already sold should give the bill to the buyer. And the counter staff cannot wipe out interest.

Begin with a call to the Assessor at 615-790-5708 and ask how your figure was built. Plenty of disagreements end in that conversation. Even so, you must reserve a hearing time with the county equalization board to protect your appeal rights. The board has five residents, each appointed by the County Commission for two years. It meets in June, and the Assessor's staff want calls during the first week of June. Filing is limited to the person on the roll, an authorized agent or the owner.

After the county hearing, the State Board of Equalization is the next step. It takes filings through August 1 of the tax year, or 45 days following the county notice when that lands later. Its administrative judge rules within 90 days of the hearing. Sales of similar homes make the strongest evidence, and a bare claim that the house is overvalued rarely succeeds. Pay the portion you do not dispute before March 1 so interest does not pile up during the appeal.

Pull together a few things before the hearing: your notice, recent sales near you, photos or repair estimates for problems the appraiser may not know about, and any recent purchase paperwork.

If your house sits in Franklin, the statement can carry county, city and Franklin Special School District charges. Read it line by line so you know which taxing body each amount belongs to, and ask the Trustee about anything that looks off.

Four programs run through the Trustee, two funded by the state, and each needs an appointment. A separate state program serves disabled former service members and their surviving spouses, so call to learn what paperwork it requires. The income test adds up 2025 earnings from every source for the applicant, spouse and co-owners. Elderly programs also require the applicant to reach 65 by the end of 2026. The tax year 2026 limits:

ProgramCombined 2025 income limit
State relief, elderly or disabled$38,470
County Broad Base relief, elderly$63,000
County Tax Freeze, age 65 or older$69,150

You apply once the 2026 bill has arrived, up to April 5, 2027, and the full tax has to be paid first. A freeze locks the home's tax at the qualifying year's level while the owner re-qualifies annually. It reaches the residence plus up to 5 acres. The locked base resets if improvements raise the value or the owner buys a different home. Call 615-790-5709 to book a slot.

The owner of record on January 1 gets the statement. If you close in the fall, the 2026 mailing still comes to you, and you need to forward it to the buyer. Your title company will show on the settlement statement how the year is split.

A simple routine works well. Before signing a contract, call the Trustee and ask what is owed on your parcel. Give the closing agent that figure, and the county gets paid from your proceeds in a single step. Keep the receipt with your closing file. If you are in the freeze program, speak to the Trustee first, since selling and then buying elsewhere resets the base amount.

Past-due tax grows with interest every month beginning March 1, and the Trustee cannot reduce it. A buyer's lender will want the account current, so clear any balance before closing. A cash buyer skips the lender's review of tax status, but the county's balance still must be settled at the table, and a cash sale can close without waiting on underwriting.

faqs.q: Where is the Williamson County Trustee's office?
faqs.a: It is in Suite 203 at 1320 West Main Street in Franklin. Staff are there weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30, and the number is 615-790-5709.

faqs.q: When does interest start on an unpaid bill?
faqs.a: Interest starts March 1, so February 28 is the final interest-free day. After that, 1.5 percent is added each month.

faqs.q: Can the Trustee forgive interest on a late bill?
faqs.a: No. State law gives the Trustee no authority to waive, prorate or release any of the tax or its interest.

faqs.q: What income cap applies to the tax freeze?
faqs.a: For tax year 2026 the cap is $69,150 of combined 2025 income for the applicant, spouse and co-owners. The applicant must also turn 65 by December 31, 2026.

faqs.q: Who do I call about an appraisal?
faqs.a: Call the Property Assessor at 615-790-5708. For the county equalization board, phone that office in the first week of June.
